stories.summary: Amit explains his system on Twitter: he has many bookmark folders, including one called 'Good Gyan' where he saves thought-provoking tweets so he can return to them later for enlightenment. He confesses, 'Guess what? I never go back, I just bookmark.' But the act of curation gave him an idea — turn the bookmarks into an episode and discuss them with Ajay live.
stories.insight: A small admission of how aspiration and reality diverge in our knowledge habits — we save more than we revisit. The salvage is to give the curated cache a second purpose by sharing it with someone else. The reader makes the tweet as much as the writer.

stories.topic: Anchal Malhotra and the Chinese Whispers of Memory
stories.summary: While researching his episode with Anchal Malhotra, who collected partition memories, Amit had a TIL: memory is not a hard drive that stores a fixed file. The first time you remember something, you go back to the event; the next time, you go back to the remembering of it; the next time, to the remembering of the remembering. It's Chinese whispers all the way down — which is why two people who shared a memory can recall it utterly differently.
stories.insight: Memory is reconstructive, not retrieval. This is a cautionary frame for how confidently we hold our autobiographical certainties — and an argument for humility when others remember the same event differently.

stories.summary: Ajay's friend, a UC Santa Cruz faculty member, took him and Ila out on a sailboat. The wind started pushing the boat away from shore. The enormity hit Ajay: 'You mean if we do absolutely nothing, the wind will just take this boat all the way out to Hawaii?' His friend said, 'Yeah, pretty much.' An eerie feeling — a boat that, untouched, would simply keep going.
stories.insight: A literal version of Faulkner's 'lose sight of the shore' — but inverted. The shore leaves you whether you intend it or not; the question is whether you'll be paying attention when it does. Often the choice is not whether to drift, but where to.

stories.topic: Bare Gulam Ali Khan and the Vegetarian Banquet
stories.summary: A Raja invites Bare Gulam Ali Khan for a Sunday performance. He arrives Friday and is hosted with the finest hospitality — except all the food is vegetarian (band gobi, aloo gobi, etc.). After the (lacklustre) Sunday performance, the Raja remarks that earlier performances Bare Gulam had given elsewhere were oceanic, magical, while today's was merely good. Bare Gulam Ali replies, in essence: when 'that' wasn't there, where would 'that' come from?
stories.insight: Inputs determine outputs in art as in life — the body is not separable from the artist. A funny, salty parable about how creators need their fuel, and how patrons who pinch on inputs deserve the outputs they get.

stories.summary: Amit was once part of a WhatsApp group of mutual acquaintances where ninety percent of the talk was bitching about other people, including mutual friends. After he left the group, he learned (unsurprised) that they had then started bitching about him.
stories.insight: Toxic-talk circles run on inertia: if you remove yourself, the circle continues, and you become the new target. The lesson is to leave anyway — surrounding yourself with complainers is a race to the bottom, and the only protection is brutal exit.

stories.topic: His Father's Death in the Second Wave Sparked the Patient-Data Idea
stories.summary: In 2021, during India's second COVID wave, Amit's father died. Talking with a friend whose father had also just died, Amit articulated the conviction that the real problem was data collection — that no one had a complete medical history of a patient in one place. He told his friend that someone should build a startup around this. He has since come to know various people doing exactly that.
stories.insight: Personal grief surfacing a systems problem — the move from individual loss to public-health design. Combined with population-scale anonymised data, the same docket also unlocks epidemiological pattern detection that no individual doctor could see.

stories.topic: Letting Go of the Shore — From 20-Minute to 10-Hour Episodes
stories.summary: When Amit started The Seen and the Unseen, he made twenty-minute episodes, because conventional thinking said attention spans were short. He has since done eight-, nine-, and ten-hour oral-history-style episodes that he would never have attempted if he had let conventional thinking hold him down.
stories.insight: The form constraints we accept are usually inherited, not validated. Doing something new usually requires letting go of the shore — falling in love with the ocean instead of the safe wisdom about what 'works.'

stories.topic: The Saturday-Evening Idea, the Sunday-Morning Column
stories.summary: Since the mid-1990s Ajay has written a fortnightly Business Standard column. His best workflow: by Saturday evening, have the idea; spend the evening reading and pushing data into his head non-purposively (no notes, no plan); sleep on it; wake up Sunday morning around 10 and write — and the clarity is dramatically better.
stories.insight: The actual learning happens during the chilling — sleep, idle time, and downtime is when neuronal connections form. Productivity, paradoxically, requires cultivating spaces where the conscious mind is not busy 'doing.'

stories.topic: The Good Gyan Episode Was Not Even Planned
stories.summary: Amit reveals that this very episode wasn't planned for the shoot. They come to the location for three days and shoot five or six episodes, often with only vague ideas — and somehow, magically, everything falls into place. The brain, once it adapts to the deadline, finds a way.
stories.insight: Creative output relies less on advance planning and more on practiced rhythms and trained brains. The deadline itself is the forcing function; the muscle memory of having done it before fills in the rest.

recommendations.item: Underrated/Overrated/Complicated episode (Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode in which they argued the underrated/overrated/complicated frame, including a discussion of social media.
recommendations.reason: Referenced as the prior conversation about social media — Ajay views Twitter as a force for bad; Amit agrees but adds nuance, and this episode resumes that conversation.

recommendations.item: Anais Nin tweet — 'We do not see things as they are. We see things as we are.'
recommendations.creator: Anais Nin (shared by Nella, @GG_dreamer)
recommendations.context: A tweet quoting Anais Nin's line on the subjectivity of perception.
recommendations.reason: The opening provocation of the episode — used to argue that perception is necessarily filtered through who we are, even when objective reality is shared.

recommendations.item: Rashomon
recommendations.creator: Akira Kurosawa
recommendations.context: Kurosawa's film in which the same event is told from different points of view.
recommendations.reason: Used as illustration of the Anais Nin point — the multiple credible versions of one event are not lies; they are how perception actually works.

recommendations.item: Anchal Malhotra episode (The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Anchal Malhotra
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with Anchal Malhotra on her partition-memories work.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Amit first encountered the reconstructive nature of memory — the Chinese-whispers framing he revisits here.

recommendations.item: Emacs
recommendations.creator: Richard Stallman
recommendations.context: The fifty-year-old text editor.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's example of the value of old, weathered tooling — its longevity has produced an elegance and bulletproof design that disposable modern code rarely achieves.

recommendations.item: The Unix episode (Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode on Unix.
recommendations.reason: Source of Ajay's earlier riff on why fifty-year-old tools (Emacs) have an elegance modern disposable code does not.

recommendations.item: Payman Milanfar tweet — 'If you're a researcher in tech and you're not reading anything older than five years, your work will be forgotten in five years.'
recommendations.creator: Payman Milanfar
recommendations.context: A tweet on the importance of reading old work in any technical field.
recommendations.reason: The tweet that opens the discussion of why even obsolete past work is worth studying — to understand how thinking in a field evolved, and to learn from people who designed under harder constraints.

recommendations.item: Shahab Bakhtiyari co-tweet on geographical reading
recommendations.creator: Shahab Bakhtiyari
recommendations.context: A co-tweet adding that the rule applies spatially — if you're not reading anything five metaphorical metres away from your discipline, your work will be forgotten five metres away.
recommendations.reason: Used to argue for interdisciplinarity not as opportunism (finding gaps at the boundaries) but as depth — narrow papers on superconductivity get read only by superconductivity people; depth comes from breadth.

recommendations.item: Constraints in Computer Technology episode (Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on the constraints under which classic computing was built.
recommendations.reason: Ajay invokes the Apollo lunar lander built with 64KB of RAM — when constraints are extreme, the people who succeed develop deep insights that disposable, resource-rich modern engineers miss.

recommendations.item: Industrial Policy episode (Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode on industrial policy.
recommendations.reason: Ajay uses the frame to critique a recent narrow-economist paper on industrial policy for developing countries — written without state-capability awareness or public-choice grounding.

recommendations.item: Ash Joglekar (Curious Wave Function) tweet on solitary hobbies
recommendations.creator: Ashutosh Joglekar
recommendations.context: A tweet arguing that solitary hobbies (reading, long-distance running, science) provide a retreat from personal and worldly tragedies.
recommendations.reason: Catalysed the episode's discussion on the importance of being alone with oneself — and the modern problem that even when alone, we are consumed in some black screen.

recommendations.item: Gurpriya Sidhu tweet — 'Be like a coach or a comrade in your professional relationships. Be like a gardener in your personal ones.'
recommendations.creator: Gurpriya Sidhu
recommendations.context: A tweet from a young writer who took Amit's clear-writing course and the Life Lessons course.
recommendations.reason: Used to draw the distinction between functional/transactional professional relationships and the open, accepting, gardener-style relationships of personal life.

recommendations.item: Life Lessons (course)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An online course taught by Amit and Ajay on lessons for living.
recommendations.reason: Amit gestures to the course's modules on learning how to learn, including the four-chunks limit on working memory and the role of downtime in consolidation.

recommendations.item: Morgan Housel tweet quoting Montesquieu
recommendations.creator: Morgan Housel
recommendations.context: Housel's tweet of Montesquieu's line: 'If you only wish to be happy, this could be easily accomplished, but if we wish to be happier than other people, this is always difficult, for we believe others to be happier than they are.'
recommendations.reason: Used to discuss the corrosive effects of comparison-driven happiness, especially after social media made everyone's curated highlight reels visible to everyone else's real selves.

recommendations.item: Morgan Housel's writing on money
recommendations.creator: Morgan Housel
recommendations.context: Generally, Housel's writing on money and human psychology.
recommendations.reason: Amit suggests Ajay should read Housel — referenced in passing as an author worth reading.

recommendations.item: Jonathan Haidt's work on social media and teenage girls
recommendations.creator: Jonathan Haidt
recommendations.context: Haidt's body of work on the harm social media does to young teenage girls.
recommendations.reason: Cited as the documented case for how the projected selves of others on social media have a particularly harmful impact on adolescent girls.

recommendations.item: Naval Ravikant — accept the whole package
recommendations.creator: Naval Ravikant
recommendations.context: Naval's line: if you envy someone for what they have, ask whether you would accept the whole package of being them — not just the achievement.
recommendations.reason: An antidote to envy. Once you ask the whole-package question, you usually find there's no one you'd actually trade places with.

recommendations.item: Maya C. Popa tweet quoting William Faulkner — 'You cannot swim for new horizons unless you have courage to lose sight of the shore.'
recommendations.creator: Maya C. Popa
recommendations.context: A tweet from poet and editor Maya C. Popa quoting Faulkner.
recommendations.reason: Anchors the episode's argument for courage — that doing something new requires letting go of the conventional shore. Maya's Twitter feed is recommended as a whole.

recommendations.item: Payman Milanfar tweet quoting Max Weber — 'I am not a donkey, I do not have a field.'
recommendations.creator: Payman Milanfar
recommendations.context: Weber's reply when asked what his field was, shared via Milanfar.
recommendations.reason: The case against academic siloing — invoked against the kind of researcher who spends ten years studying wheat production in Arizona in 1853 without seeing the bigger picture.

recommendations.item: Vijayendra Rao paper / EIE episode on reflexive economics
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode discussing Vijayendra (Biju) Rao's paper on how economics, sociology and anthropology have all gone into silos and how economics should be more reflexive.
recommendations.reason: Used to extend the Weber point — that even within an academic discipline, sub-silos prevent the bigger picture from emerging.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal tweet on complaining
recommendations.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: A tweet: 'An easy way to become less unlikable is to stop complaining. If you have a problem, fix it. If you need help, ask for it. But if your problem is beyond anyone's control, then complaining about it does nothing but pollute the atmosphere with bitterness.'
recommendations.reason: Becomes a launching point for Amit's near-mission-statement against negativity in his own life, and the brutal exit from toxic groups.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal episode (The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: Amit's two-hour episode with Gurwinder Bhogal.
recommendations.reason: Bhogal made a reputation on Twitter through mega-threads of original synthesis; Amit recommends his earlier S&U appearance for the longer conversation.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal's Substack
recommendations.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: Bhogal's long-form Substack writings.
recommendations.reason: Recommended as the place to read Bhogal's longer-form synthesis when 280 characters isn't enough.

recommendations.item: Serenity Prayer — 'God, give me the strength to change the things I can, the serenity to accept the things I can't, and the wisdom to know the difference.'
recommendations.creator: Reinhold Niebuhr (Christian sources)
recommendations.context: The classic prayer offered as an antidote to whining.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's framing for treating the world as a fixed field on which only your levers, resources, and agency matter. Everything else is conversation.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal tweet on tribal certainty
recommendations.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: Tweet: 'If you learn about an issue people have been debating for ages and conclude that the answer is obvious and one side is just stupid or evil, you haven't expanded your mind to grasp the issue, you've shrunk the issue to fit your mind.'
recommendations.reason: A diagnostic for tribalism. The moment you take the tribal line, you have confessed that you no longer care about the truth — you care about your team.

recommendations.item: Visakan Veerasamy tweet quoting Nietzsche — 'He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how.'
recommendations.creator: Visakan Veerasamy
recommendations.context: A tweet from one of the more interesting thinkers Amit follows on Twitter.
recommendations.reason: Springboard for the discussion of purpose as superpower — practical aspects are solvable; the fire is what keeps you going.

recommendations.item: Bhagavad Gita — duty without attachment to fruits
recommendations.creator: Vyasa (traditional)
recommendations.context: The Gita's framework for action without attachment to outcomes.
recommendations.reason: Ajay invokes it to marry purpose with happiness — you are obliged to try, but you don't control external outcomes; distancing from the fruit is what saves a purposeful life from being a miserable one.

recommendations.item: Delano Sullivan tweet quoting Matt Kahn — 'People can only meet you as deeply as they've met themselves.'
recommendations.creator: Delano Sullivan
recommendations.context: A tweet from a young curator of literature on Twitter (handle @DelanoA4).
recommendations.reason: Argues that the only path to understanding another person is to first understand yourself — the layers of self-knowledge are the layers of other-knowledge.

recommendations.item: Delano Sullivan tweet quoting Schopenhauer on the art of not reading
recommendations.creator: Delano Sullivan
recommendations.context: Schopenhauer: 'The art of not reading is a very important one. It consists in not taking an interest in whatever may be engaging the attention of the general public at any particular time... A precondition for reading good books is not reading bad ones, for life is short.'
recommendations.reason: Compressed by Ajay to a bumper-sticker — 'Don't follow anybody on Twitter.' A defence of curating inputs aggressively.

recommendations.item: Lancelot Pinto episode (The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lancelot Pinto
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with the Bombay pulmonologist Lancelot Pinto.
recommendations.reason: Pinto reads new papers every day and is an example of the rare doctor genuinely keeping up. He is also writing a book that Amit predicts will still be read fifty years from now.

recommendations.item: Abby Phillips (Liver Doc) episode (The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Abby Phillips
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Liver Doc Abby Phillips.
recommendations.reason: Phillips is the other doctor on Amit's show who reads literature continuously — held up as the rare exception against most Indian doctors who do not.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal tweet on AI making us machine-like
recommendations.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: Tweet: 'The better AI gets at doing our work for us, the more we outsource our thinking to it. As we make machines more human-like, they make us more machine-like. Perhaps we should be less worried about AI becoming conscious than about humanity becoming unconscious.'
recommendations.reason: Used to argue not against AI but against treating AI as a crutch — let it be a tool that enhances thinking, not a substitute for it.

recommendations.item: Sahil Bloom tweet on planning vs preparation
recommendations.creator: Sahil Bloom
recommendations.context: Tweet: 'Preparation always beats planning. Planning is based on the expectation of order. Preparation is based on the expectation of chaos.'
recommendations.reason: Anchors the planning-vs-preparation distinction — invoked alongside Tyson's 'everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth' and the planning-is-everything line.

recommendations.item: The 5 Types of Wealth
recommendations.creator: Sahil Bloom
recommendations.context: Sahil Bloom's then-forthcoming book on the five kinds of wealth.
recommendations.reason: Mentioned by Amit as sitting in his Kindle queue at the time of recording, expected to be read by telecast.

recommendations.item: LYN tweet — 'Too broke to smoke crack, gotta get up and make it happen.'
recommendations.creator: LYN
recommendations.context: A tweet Amit names as one of his all-time favourites.
recommendations.reason: If you want something badly enough — addictively enough — you will find a way. The same energy as a dope head wanting crack, channelled into a creative life.

recommendations.item: Pico Iyer tweet quoting Rousseau
recommendations.creator: Pico Iyer
recommendations.context: Iyer's tweet of Rousseau: 'Real wisdom is not the knowledge of everything, but the knowledge of which things in life are necessary, which are less necessary, and which are completely unnecessary to know.' Iyer adds: for that, you have to put your phone away.
recommendations.reason: A clean closer to the episode's curation theme — and a teasing barb at Ajay, who had been on his phone for half an hour beforehand taking calls about markets.

recommendations.item: Paul Graham's essays
recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Graham's full essays page online.
recommendations.reason: Amit's standing recommendation — many Paul Graham tweets are in his Good Gyan folder; the essays are 'just one of the greatest essays ever' written. The next Good Gyan episode will surely include him.

core_ideas.concept: Twitter as a Curation Device, Not a Cesspool
core_ideas.explanation: Used well, Twitter is the privilege of having the best minds in the world think aloud for your benefit every morning. The retweet button and the like button broke our discourse by amplifying tribalism and validation-seeking, but a curated feed and a folder system (e.g. 'Good Gyan' bookmarks) flips the ratio. The reader makes the tweet as much as the writer.
core_ideas.quote: If you curate your feed well, you are actually getting the privilege to listen to the best minds in the world think aloud for your benefit every morning.

core_ideas.concept: We Do Not See Things as They Are; We See Them as We Are
core_ideas.explanation: Anais Nin's line as a frame for perception. The world has objective facts (a chair is a chair, blackbody radiation has a fixed spectrum), but how we make sense of complex experience depends fundamentally on who is doing the perceiving. Rashomon is not a story about unreliable memory; it's a story about how perception works. The caution: don't be quick to judge — you are part of the equation.
core_ideas.quote: We do not see things as they are. We see things as we are. — Anais Nin

core_ideas.explanation: Memory is not a hard drive that stores a fixed file. The first remembering goes back to the event; the next goes back to the first remembering; the third goes back to the second remembering. Each pass is a partial reconstruction with edits. Two people can therefore recall the same shared moment in incompatible ways, both honestly. This is why autobiographical certainty deserves humility.

Ajay's conscientious objection: yes, perception is slippery, but there is such a thing as objective knowledge, and pursuing it is what makes us human. Planck's blackbody formula is correct to the last decimal. We must hold shades of grey around contested claims while not surrendering the project of truth. If we accept that 'everyone has their own truth,' we open the door to every conspiracy theory. The Sisyphean uphill journey is the point.
core_ideas.quote: If you prick us, do we not bleed? — Shakespeare's Shylock, invoked against post-truth relativism.

core_ideas.concept: Read the Old, Read the Far
core_ideas.explanation: Payman Milanfar's tech-research rule: 'If you're not reading anything older than five years, your work will be forgotten in five years.' Shahab Bakhtiyari's spatial extension: the same applies metaphorically across disciplines and geographies. Old work survives because it was hammered out under harder constraints (64KB RAM and an Apollo lunar lander). Distant work survives because depth of any one field requires breadth across many. The Chinese DeepSeek team's success is partly the payoff of taking both rules seriously.
core_ideas.quote: I am not a donkey, I do not have a field. — Max Weber

core_ideas.concept: Architect vs Gardener (and Cooking vs Gardening)
core_ideas.explanation: Two metaphors for creative work, on a continuum. The architect plans every room of the house and then builds — the way some plot-driven crime novels are written, or the young-male top-down view of running a firm (whip the ingredients together like cooking). The gardener starts with shrubbery and bushes, prunes, and lets shape emerge — the way most great novelists actually work, and the way Shovam Mishra describes a firm. Even within architecting, you garden a room; even within gardening, you architect the bed. The gardener mode also applies to your inner life — talking to yourself with depth so the exterior can have depth.
core_ideas.quote: When you're talking to yourself, you should be talking to yourself as if you're gardening.

core_ideas.concept: Comparison Is the Thief of Happiness (and Selfishness Is the Cure)
core_ideas.explanation: Montesquieu's frame: if we only wished to be happy it would be easy, but we wish to be happier than others, which is always difficult — because we believe others to be happier than they are. Social media puts our real selves in competition with other people's projected selves. Ajay's prescription: a productive selfishness — be busy with your own striving, your own writing, your own building, and the bandwidth for envy disappears. Naval's antidote: ask whether you'd accept the whole package of being the person you envy. Usually no.
core_ideas.quote: Resentment is like taking poison and hoping the other person dies.

core_ideas.explanation: Working memory holds about four chunks at a time; effortful focus saturates fast and dead-ends in frustration. The actual consolidation — the connection-making between distributed parts of the brain — happens in the rest, the walks, the showers, and the sleep. Hence Ajay's column workflow: by Saturday evening, have the idea; spend the evening pushing data into your head non-purposively; sleep; write Sunday morning with dramatic clarity. Productivity needs gardens of unscheduled time, not a calendar painted black.
core_ideas.quote: The learning happens where you're chilling, you're not even thinking about it consciously.

core_ideas.explanation: Gurwinder Bhogal's rule: if you can fix it, fix it; if you need help, ask for it; if it's beyond control, complaining only pollutes the atmosphere. The corollary at the social level: cut out chronic complainers — the WhatsApp groups whose ninety percent talk is bitching, the Twitter circles whose dunks are screenshots. They will bitch about you the moment you leave. Surround yourself with people who, when you share an idea, help you build it instead of telling you why it won't work.

core_ideas.concept: Emotional Encouragement at the Point of Inception
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's rule: when someone in your circle comes up with an idea, support it. Later you will have fifteen criticisms and improvements. But at the moment of inception, the first response disproportionately determines whether the idea survives at all. We are made out of the responses that other people give our ideas — so creating depends on cultures and communities that embrace and push each other's projects rather than puncture them.
core_ideas.quote: Emotional encouragement is just so disproportionately important at the point of inception.

core_ideas.concept: Tribal Certainty Is the Confession of Having Stopped Caring About Truth
core_ideas.explanation: Bhogal again: if you learn about an issue people have debated for ages and decide one side is just stupid or evil, you haven't expanded your mind to grasp the issue, you've shrunk the issue to fit your mind. The moment you take the tribal line on a complex question, you are confessing you no longer care about truth — you care about belonging. (Some questions are settled — the earth is round; nationalism and militarism are not.)

core_ideas.concept: Purpose as the Why That Makes Any How Bearable
core_ideas.explanation: Nietzsche: 'He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how.' Purpose is the superpower because the practical aspects — projects, resources, logistics — are solvable. The fire is what keeps you going through the long game when there's no immediate gratification. To avoid the burden side of purpose, marry it to the Bhagavad Gita's injunction: you are obliged to try, but you don't control outcomes. Without that distance from the fruit of labour, big purposes set you up for big pain.

Sahil Bloom: planning expects order; preparation expects chaos. Tyson: everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth. Eisenhower (paraphrased): plans are useless, but planning is everything. Good military planning doesn't predict the campaign — it imagines many scenarios and prepares the mind with contingency, logistics, and the certainty that the other guy gets a vote. The years of gym work, not the fight-night plan, are what survive the first punch.
core_ideas.quote: Plans are useless, but planning is everything.

core_ideas.concept: If You Need to Ask, the Answer Is No
core_ideas.explanation: When aspiring writers ask Amit whether they should write a book, the answer is always no — because if you have to ask, you don't want it badly enough. The threshold is addictive desire: 'too broke to smoke crack, gotta get up and make it happen.' Reminding yourself of mortality can manufacture the urgency. The artists who finish are the ones who can't not.

core_ideas.concept: The Doctor-Patient Knowledge Hierarchy and the Indian AI Opportunity
core_ideas.explanation: Patients fall into two camps — those who read Google and those who read Google Scholar — and so do doctors, with most reading neither. Lancelot Pinto and Abby Phillips read papers daily; most Indian doctors don't, which makes outdated knowledge the norm (in nutrition, anything older than five years can be positively harmful). The opportunity: a model where nurses do the multi-hour patient-history docket, the docket goes to an AI in formal structure, and the AI's diagnostic output beats most doctors of the world. Combined with anonymised population data, this is also how Indian public health gets its pattern-detection layer.
core_ideas.quote: Patients come in two categories: those that read Google, and those that read Google Scholar.

core_ideas.explanation: Faulkner's line, applied to creative work and to life. Doing anything new requires getting the ballast of conventional thinking out of the way. Amit started The Seen and the Unseen with twenty-minute episodes because conventional wisdom said attention spans were short; the eight-, nine-, and ten-hour episodes that became his signature would not exist if he had let that wisdom hold him. The shore is the safe form, the inherited constraint. The ocean is everything else.
core_ideas.quote: You cannot swim for new horizons unless you have courage to lose sight of the shore. — William Faulkner

core_ideas.explanation: The better AI gets at doing our work, the more we are tempted to outsource thinking to it; the danger isn't AI becoming conscious, it's humanity becoming unconscious. Ajay's optimism: creative sparks come from places deep in the human mind that nothing understands; AI handling tasks just frees humans to create. Amit's caveat applies to any technology: let it enhance what you can do, don't stop thinking just because perplexity knows everything.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on his Good Gyan bookmark folder: 'I save it... I'm gonna get enlightened. Guess what? I never go back, I just bookmark.'

Amit accusing Ajay of taking everything literally: '[earlier] you took it [spatial reading] metaphorically. Here I thought I'm being metaphorical, I think Faulkner was being metaphorical, but you went literally — actually the shore was going away.'

Ajay on novelists: 'So you mean novelists don't start with a spreadsheet of all the characters and their characteristics.' Amit: 'Oh my god, this is what you would do, isn't it, Ajay-sa? Please remain an economist.'
